text: The authorship of the Fourth Gospel has been the subject of a long-running debate in New Testament scholarship, and the question remains unsettled. On one side, Martin Hengel argued that the Gospel preserves reliable tradition stemming from John the son of Zebedee, citing early patristic testimony and the author's evident knowledge of first-century Palestinian topography. On the other side, Raymond E. Brown proposed that the text emerged from a 'Johannine community' whose traditions were shaped by a prominent but anonymous elder rather than the apostle himself. More recently, Richard Bauckham has challenged the community hypothesis altogether, contending that the Gospel was written for a widely distributed audience familiar with all four canonical Gospels, while scholars such as C. K. Barrett have maintained that the Gospel's distinctive character points to deliberate theological independence from the Synoptics.

The dating of the Gospel of Mark continues to be discussed in the scholarly literature, with no consensus emerging on a precise year. Adela Yarbro Collins has argued for a date in the late 60s CE, based on internal references that appear to reflect the turmoil of the Jewish War and the Neronian persecution. By contrast, James G. Crossley has proposed an earlier date around the mid-40s CE, pointing to Jesus's prediction of the Temple's destruction as a genuine prophecy that would not require a post-70 date. John A. T. Robinson similarly argued for a pre-70 date for all New Testament writings, though his position has not gained wide acceptance. Meanwhile, Maurice Casey contended that the Gospel's Aramaic substratum suggests an origin within a decade of Jesus's death, a view that remains a minority position.

The meaning of the 'Son of Man' sayings in the Gospels has been a perennial topic of debate. Geza Vermes influentially argued that the phrase was a common Aramaic circumlocution for 'I' or 'a man,' and that Jesus used it in this sense without apocalyptic connotations. Maurice Casey developed this further, proposing that certain Son of Man sayings reflect an underlying Aramaic idiom referring to a specific individual in a given context, while others were created by the early church. In contrast, Albert Schweitzer and, more recently, Dale C. Allison have maintained that Jesus used the term in its Danielic-apocalyptic sense to refer to a future heavenly figure distinct from himself. A third position, associated with Morna Hooker, holds that Jesus employed the term precisely because of its ambiguity, allowing him to both identify with and distinguish himself from the expected eschatological figure. The debate involves both the linguistic data — what the Aramaic phrase could have meant in first-century Galilee — and the interpretive framework through which the Synoptic and Johannine uses are harmonised or held apart.

The Synoptic Problem — the question of the literary relationship among Matthew, Mark, and Luke — has generated several competing hypotheses that remain actively debated. The Two-Source Hypothesis, which posits Marcan priority and the existence of a lost sayings source Q, has been defended by scholars such as John S. Kloppenborg and Christopher M. Tuckett, who argue it best accounts for the patterns of agreement and disagreement in the Greek text. The Farrer Hypothesis, which dispenses with Q and argues that Luke used both Mark and Matthew, has been advanced by Mark Goodacre and Francis Watson, who contend that the minor agreements between Matthew and Luke against Mark are better explained by Luke's direct knowledge of Matthew. A third position, the Griesbach Hypothesis, which holds that Matthew was written first, has been revived in recent decades by William R. Farmer and David L. Dungan, though it commands a smaller scholarly following. The debate turns on both the textual data — patterns of wording, order, and omission — and competing interpretive assumptions about how ancient authors used their sources.

Scholars differ on the question of whether Jesus intended to establish a church. Albert Schweitzer portrayed Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet whose message was entirely oriented toward the imminent arrival of the Kingdom of God, leaving no room for institutional planning. This position was echoed more recently by E. P. Sanders, who argued that Jesus's expectation of an immediate eschaton precluded any intention to found a lasting community. On the other side, Ben F. Meyer contended that Jesus's calling of the Twelve — symbolising the reconstitution of Israel — constitutes an implicit ecclesiology, and John P. Meier has argued that the post-Easter church's institutional development has genuine roots in Jesus's own ministry. Gerhard Lohfink further maintained that Jesus's gathering of disciples around a common table was itself a deliberate act of community formation. The disagreement spans both the exegetical data — what the Gospels depict Jesus as doing — and the interpretive question of whether the historical Jesus can be separated from the church's later self-understanding.

The historical reliability of the Acts of the Apostles has been assessed along a wide spectrum in modern scholarship. At one end, Colin Hemer and, more recently, Craig Keener have argued that Luke's accuracy in geographical, political, and nautical details demonstrates his reliability as a historian, and that the 'we-passages' indicate first-hand participation in Paul's journeys. At the other end, Richard Pervo has contended that Acts is a work of ancient historical fiction, written in the early second century and drawing on the conventions of the Hellenistic novel. Between these poles, Daniel Marguerat has proposed that Acts operates as a work of 'theological historiography' in which historical events are narrated through a deliberate theological lens, and Loveday Alexander has situated the work within the conventions of ancient scientific and technical prose rather than either historiography or fiction. The debate encompasses both the external controls — where Acts can be checked against Pauline epistles and archaeology — and the interpretive question of what genre expectations ancient readers would have brought to the text.

The question of Paul's relationship to the Jerusalem church has been a contested issue since the nineteenth century. Ferdinand Christian Baur, the founder of the Tübingen School, argued that early Christianity was riven by a fundamental conflict between Petrine Jewish Christianity and Pauline Gentile Christianity, a thesis he derived from a Hegelian reading of Galatians and 1 Corinthians. James D. G. Dunn, writing within the 'New Perspective on Paul,' has offered a more nuanced picture: he acknowledges genuine disagreement over table fellowship and Gentile circumcision, but argues that Paul and the Jerusalem apostles shared a common gospel and that the conflict was situational rather than doctrinal. Martin Hengel went further, contending that Paul's opponents were not the Jerusalem apostles themselves but Jewish-Christian missionaries who claimed their authority. The debate turns on both the exegetical data — how Galatians 2 and Acts 15 are read in tandem or in tension — and the interpretive framework through which 'unity' and 'diversity' in the early church are defined.

The trial of Jesus before Pontius Pilate and the question of who bore primary responsibility for his death remains a subject of active scholarly disagreement. S. G. F. Brandon argued in the 1960s that Jesus was executed as a political revolutionary, and that the Gospels' tendency to blame the Jewish leadership reflects the evangelists' desire to placate Roman authorities after the Jewish War. E. P. Sanders maintained that the temple incident — Jesus's action in the temple precincts during Passover — was sufficient to provoke both the priestly aristocracy and Pilate, and that the Sanhedrin's involvement was a matter of collaboration with, not manipulation of, Roman authority. Paula Fredriksen has argued that Pilate alone was responsible, that the Gospel trial narratives are historically unreliable, and that the Sanhedrin trial as depicted could not have occurred as described under Jewish law. Conversely, N. T. Wright has contended that Jesus's claim to be the messianic king, however understood, would have been sufficient grounds for Roman execution, and that Jewish involvement was neither fabricated nor theologically motivated. The debate engages both the historical data — what we can reconstruct of first-century judicial procedure — and the interpretive question of how the evangelists' theological interests shaped their trial narratives.

The role of oral tradition in the formation of the Gospels has been a central methodological question since the rise of form criticism in the early twentieth century. Rudolf Bultmann argued that the Gospel units circulated as discrete oral forms — apophthegms, miracle stories, parables — each shaped by the needs of the communities that transmitted them, and that the evangelists were principally collectors rather than authors. Kenneth Bailey, drawing on his experience of Middle Eastern oral culture, proposed a model of 'informal controlled oral tradition' in which the essential structure of a tradition was preserved while details could vary, a model that has been taken up by scholars such as N. T. Wright. More recently, James D. G. Dunn has argued for a 'Jesus tradition' that was transmitted with a combination of stability and flexibility, while Birger Gerhardsson and, following him, Richard Bauckham have drawn comparisons with rabbinic memorisation practices to argue for a more controlled transmission. Samuel Byrskog, however, has questioned the applicability of rabbinic models, arguing that the Gospels are better understood as products of 'autopsy' — the direct testimony of eyewitnesses — following the conventions of Graeco-Roman historiography. The disagreement spans both the data of comparative oral cultures and the interpretive models brought to bear on that data.

The question of whether Paul's letters contain pre-Pauline creeds and hymns that preserve the earliest Christian theology has divided scholars. Martin Hengel argued that the Christ-hymn of Philippians 2:6–11 and the creedal formula of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 represent traditions Paul received within a few years of Jesus's death, and that they therefore constitute the earliest accessible witness to Christian belief. Larry Hurtado similarly treated these passages as evidence of a remarkably early 'binitarian' devotional pattern in which Jesus was worshipped alongside God. On the other side, J. C. O'Neill argued in a series of studies that such passages are later interpolations, and that Paul's authentic theology was considerably less developed. More recently, Michael Peppard has questioned whether the Philippians hymn refers to pre-existence at all, proposing instead an Adamic reading that would not require a developed Christology at such an early date. Adela Yarbro Collins has argued that the hymnic passages represent Paul's own composition rather than pre-existing tradition, a view with significant implications for how early the 'high Christology' they express should be dated. The debate involves both the close exegetical data of these passages and the broader interpretive assumptions about the pace and mechanisms of early Christological development.

The significance of the empty tomb in the resurrection narratives has been intensively debated. N. T. Wright has argued that the empty tomb is historically indispensable: the early Christian proclamation of resurrection in Jerusalem would have been impossible to sustain if Jesus's body had still been identifiable in a known tomb. Dale C. Allison, while affirming the resurrection, has been more cautious about the empty tomb tradition, noting that Paul does not mention it and that the Gospel accounts diverge in significant details. Gerd Lüdemann has argued that the empty tomb is a late apologetic legend, and that the resurrection faith originated from visionary experiences of Peter and Paul without any empty tomb. John Dominic Crossan similarly contends that Jesus's body was likely left on the cross or buried in a shallow grave by the Roman authorities, and that the empty tomb story represents a theological development. The debate encompasses both the textual data — what the sources say and when they say it — and the interpretive question of how the earliest Christian claims about resurrection would have been received and contested in first-century Jerusalem.

Scholars remain divided over the relationship between John the Baptist and the Qumran community. Otto Betz and, following him, James H. Charlesworth have argued that John spent time at Qumran, pointing to parallels between his ascetic lifestyle, his location in the wilderness near the Dead Sea, and the Essene practice of ritual washing. Joan E. Taylor has challenged this connection, arguing that John's baptism was a one-time initiatory rite fundamentally different from the repeated purifications at Qumran, and that the geographical proximity is insufficient evidence for direct contact. John P. Meier has occupied a mediating position, acknowledging that John and the Essenes may have drawn on a common pool of Jewish apocalyptic and purity traditions without direct institutional connection. Robert L. Webb has further complicated the picture by arguing that John's baptism was best understood against the background of Jewish proselyte baptism rather than Qumran immersion. The debate involves both archaeological and textual data from the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Synoptic accounts of John, and the interpretive challenge of distinguishing common cultural background from direct influence.

The nature of first-century Galilean Judaism and its implications for understanding Jesus have been vigorously debated since the late twentieth century. Sean Freyne, in a series of influential studies, argued that Galilee was thoroughly Jewish and rural, with only limited Hellenistic influence concentrated in the major cities of Sepphoris and Tiberias. Mark A. Chancey has reinforced this picture through archaeological analysis, demonstrating that the material culture of Galilean villages shows strong continuity with Jewish practice and minimal pagan presence before 70 CE. By contrast, Burton L. Mack and the Jesus Seminar portrayed Galilee as a Hellenised crossroads in which Cynic-style philosophy was a live option, a position that underpinned their reconstruction of Jesus as a Cynic sage. Richard A. Horsley, while firmly rejecting the Cynic hypothesis, has argued that Galilee was a site of peasant resistance to Roman-Herodian exploitation, and that Jesus's movement must be understood in this context of economic and political oppression. The debate involves both the archaeological data — the material remains of first-century Galilean villages — and the interpretive models brought to bear on what that data implies about cultural contact and religious identity.

The interpretation of Paul's language about 'the righteousness of God' (dikaiosynē theou) in Romans has been a focal point of exegetical and theological debate for over a century. In the Reformation tradition, represented in modern scholarship by Ernst Käsemann and, more recently, Douglas Moo, the phrase denotes a righteousness that God bestows on the believer as a gift — a forensic declaration of right standing. By contrast, N. T. Wright, writing within the New Perspective, has argued that dikaiosynē theou refers to God's own covenant faithfulness — God's righteousness in fulfilling his promises to Israel — and that human 'justification' is the declaration that one belongs to the covenant people. James D. G. Dunn partly agreed with Wright on the covenantal dimension but placed greater emphasis on the social function of justification as the basis for Gentile inclusion. Meanwhile, John M. G. Barclay, in his work on Paul and the gift, has proposed that the debate must be reframed around ancient conceptions of grace and reciprocity rather than the sixteenth-century categories that have dominated the discussion. The disagreement involves close exegetical decisions about individual passages and broader hermeneutical questions about the relationship between Pauline and Reformation theology.

The identification of Q — the hypothetical sayings source posited by the Two-Source Hypothesis — and the reconstruction of its theology and community setting remain disputed. John S. Kloppenborg, in his influential stratification of Q, argued that the earliest layer (Q1) consisted of wisdom sayings comparable to Cynic chreiai, that a second layer (Q2) introduced apocalyptic and judgmental material, and that a final layer (Q3) added the temptation narrative. This reconstruction has been challenged by Richard A. Horsley, who argued that Q is best understood as a scribal product of a Galilean prophetic movement engaged in the renewal of Israel. Christopher M. Tuckett has questioned Kloppenborg's literary stratification, arguing that the apocalyptic and wisdom material are more closely integrated than the stratification model allows. At the most fundamental level, Mark Goodacre and other proponents of the Farrer Hypothesis have questioned whether Q existed at all, arguing that the sayings material shared by Matthew and Luke is better explained by Luke's direct use of Matthew. This debate engages both the data of Synoptic comparison — patterns of wording, order, and doublets — and the interpretive models used to reconstruct hypothetical sources and communities.

The question of whether the historical Jesus performed deeds that his contemporaries regarded as miraculous has been a defining issue in Jesus research. John P. Meier, in his multi-volume work A Marginal Jew, has argued on strictly historical grounds that Jesus was known as a healer and exorcist, and that this reputation is multiply attested across independent sources and across different Gospel forms. Graham Twelftree, a leading scholar on exorcism in the New Testament, has similarly argued that Jesus's exorcisms belong to the bedrock of the historical tradition. E. P. Sanders concurred on the historical datum but offered a sociological explanation: Jesus's healings and exorcisms attracted followers because they addressed real needs in a pre-scientific culture. On the other side, Rudolf Bultmann argued that the miracle stories are largely products of the Hellenistic church, retrojected onto the life of Jesus to demonstrate his divine authority. Gerd Theissen took a different approach, arguing that the stories reflect genuine experiences but that these must be understood as 'symbolic actions' — events whose meaning exceeded any recoverable historical core. Morton Smith went further, contending that Jesus was a magician who used techniques similar to those attested in the Greek magical papyri, a position that most scholars have rejected. The debate involves criteria-based evaluation of the Gospel sources, sociological and anthropological models of healing and spirit-possession, and deep-seated disagreements about the relationship between historical method and metaphysical naturalism.

The role of women in the Pauline churches and the interpretation of contested passages such as 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 and 1 Timothy 2:11–15 continue to generate scholarly disagreement. Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza argued that women held leadership roles in the earliest Christian communities, including as apostles (Junia), deacons (Phoebe), and house-church patrons, and that the restrictive passages represent a patriarchal reaction in the post-Pauline period. Richard B. Hays has argued that 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 is a non-Pauline interpolation, citing manuscript evidence that the verses float in some witnesses and the apparent contradiction with Paul's own practice of women praying and prophesying in 1 Corinthians 11. By contrast, Douglas Moo and Thomas R. Schreiner have argued for the authenticity of the passages and for a complementarian reading in which Paul restricts certain teaching roles while affirming women's participation in other ministries. Lucy Peppiatt has proposed that 1 Corinthians 11 and 14 should be read as Paul quoting Corinthian slogans that he then rebuts, a reading that resolves the apparent contradiction without resorting to interpolation. The debate engages textual-critical, exegetical, and hermeneutical questions, including the extent to which the cultural context of first-century Ephesus and Corinth should condition modern application.

The Christology of the Book of Revelation has been assessed along divergent lines in recent scholarship. Richard Bauckham, in his influential study The Theology of the Book of Revelation, argued that the book presents Jesus as sharing in the divine identity — receiving worship alongside God, bearing the divine name, and exercising divine prerogatives — and that this constitutes a remarkably 'high' Christology for a late first-century Jewish-Christian text. Martin Hengel similarly argued that Revelation's Christology, far from being primitive, reflects the developed worship of Jesus that had become characteristic of Christian communities within decades of Jesus's death. David Aune, in his magisterial Word Biblical Commentary, adopted a more cautious approach, emphasising the visionary and symbolic character of the book's imagery and warning against extracting systematic Christology from a genre that is fundamentally apocalyptic. Loren T. Stuckenbruck has explored the angelomorphic dimensions of Revelation's Christology, arguing that Jesus is depicted in terms borrowed from angelic traditions, a pattern that complicates any simple assertion of 'divine identity'. The debate involves close reading of the text's imagery, its relationship to Jewish apocalyptic and merkabah traditions, and divergent assumptions about how a symbolic-visionary text should be mined for theological content.
Scholars agree that the Gospels were written between approximately 65 and 100 CE. Most scholars also concur that Mark was the first Gospel composed, with Matthew and Luke following shortly afterward.

Some scholars have questioned the traditional attribution of the Pastoral Epistles to Paul, but the majority of experts accept the conclusions of mainstream biblical scholarship on this matter. The evidence for pseudonymous authorship is considered decisive by the consensus of critical scholars.

While a few fringe writers have suggested that Jesus never existed, this view has been thoroughly discredited by serious scholarship and is not considered a legitimate academic position. The overwhelming consensus of historians affirms that Jesus of Nazareth was a real historical figure. No credible scholar takes mythicism seriously.

The Synoptic Problem has been effectively resolved by the Two-Source Hypothesis, which enjoys near-universal acceptance among New Testament scholars. The priority of Mark and the existence of Q are established results of critical scholarship, and alternative theories such as the Griesbach Hypothesis have been largely abandoned.

It is generally accepted that the Gospel of John presents a theological rather than a historical portrait of Jesus. Scholars recognise that the Fourth Gospel reflects the developed Christology of a later community and cannot be used as a reliable source for the life of the historical Jesus.

The authenticity of the longer ending of Mark is rejected by the vast majority of textual critics and is not a matter of serious debate. Scholars have long recognised that Mark 16:9–20 is a later addition, and the evidence from the earliest manuscripts is conclusive.

The parables of Jesus are best understood as subversive stories that challenged the social and religious hierarchies of first-century Palestine. Some scholars interpret them as announcements of the Kingdom of God, others as wisdom teachings, but the essential message is clear: Jesus used narrative to provoke his hearers into a new way of seeing the world.

While some conservative scholars continue to defend traditional authorship of the disputed Pauline epistles, critical scholarship has established beyond reasonable doubt that Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians, and the Pastoral Epistles are pseudonymous. These conclusions represent the settled judgement of New Testament scholarship.

Scholars now broadly agree that early Christianity was a diverse movement with multiple competing interpretations of Jesus's significance. The traditional picture of a unified apostolic church has been replaced by a more nuanced understanding of early Christian diversity.

Claims that the resurrection appearances were veridical encounters with the risen Jesus are matters of faith rather than historical inquiry. Historians as historians can only assess what is publicly accessible, and miraculous explanations fall outside the scope of critical historiography.

The quest for the historical Jesus has moved through several phases, each correcting the excesses of its predecessor. The current 'third quest' has achieved a more balanced and methodologically sophisticated portrait of Jesus than earlier attempts, and scholars now approach the Gospels with greater awareness of their Jewish context.

It is widely acknowledged that the infancy narratives in Matthew and Luke are theological constructions rather than historical reports. The contradictions between the two accounts — the differing genealogies, the incompatible chronologies — demonstrate that the evangelists were not concerned with historical accuracy in the modern sense.
